question: Why did Next.js transition from middleware.ts to proxy.ts?
options: To clarify its role as a network boundary layer and run on the standard Node.js runtime by default instead of a constrained Edge environment
To execute routing logic inside the user's browser Service Worker before requests reach the server
To automatically encrypt all SQL queries inside Client Components without a Data Access Layer
To replace Server Actions as the primary place where form mutations write to the database
explanation: Renaming middleware.ts to proxy.ts makes the network boundary explicit and shifts execution to the full Node.js runtime, eliminating Edge API compatibility issues.

question: What happens in the user's browser address bar when proxy.ts returns a rewrite for acme.app.local/settings to /tenants/acme/settings?
options: The browser address bar changes to acme.app.local/tenants/acme/settings via an HTTP 307 redirect
The browser address bar stays at acme.app.local/settings while Next.js internally renders the /tenants/acme/settings route
Next.js blocks the request because rewrites cannot cross dynamic route segments
The browser reloads the page twice to synchronize the pathname with the server
explanation: A proxy rewrite maps an incoming URL to an internal destination transparently on the server without changing the URL visible in the browser.

question: Why is relying solely on proxy.ts for authentication and authorization considered an anti-pattern?
options: Because proxy.ts cannot read request cookies or headers on incoming HTTP requests
Because matcher misconfigurations or optimistic cookie checks at the proxy boundary cannot replace authoritative role and tenant verification at the Data Access Layer and Server Actions
Because proxy.ts only executes during static build generation and never runs at request time
Because NextResponse.redirect automatically grants admin privileges to subsequent requests
explanation: Defense-in-depth requires verifying sessions, roles, and tenant ownership inside your DAL and Server Actions so that a matcher mistake or stale cookie at the proxy boundary never exposes sensitive data.

question: Why should static asset paths like /_next/static and /favicon.ico be excluded from proxy execution?
options: Because static assets are served only over WebSockets
To avoid running proxy logic, header allocation, and redirect checks on every static asset request
Because Next.js deletes static files if they pass through proxy.ts
Because browsers refuse to parse CSS files that contain custom response headers
explanation: Skipping /_next assets and /favicon.ico prevents unnecessary compute and latency overhead on high-volume static asset requests.
